plan.title: Asked for a video link: a YouTube search phrase, no link, nothing invented

transcript.text:
Hey, I'm ZOH! I'll help you get better at one thing with a small step each day. Text "stop" anytime, and you can change how I coach whenever you want, just say "chill out" or "push me harder."

What's your name, and what are you looking to work on?

• Put AI to work for you
• Read & learn more (books, ideas, any topic)
• Start something on the side
• Focus & get more done
• Speak & connect better
• Get fitter
• Eat better
• Sleep better
• Learn a fun skill (Rubik's cube, card trick, play a song, drawing)
• Not sure? Let's figure it out together
Let's go, Dana! What kind of movement do you enjoy, or have you done before, like gym, walking, running, or home workouts?
I want to learn proper squats and deadlifts, never lifted before
Love that, Dana. Squats and deadlifts are a great place to start, and we'll build the form from zero. Where will you practice: a gym you already have, or at home?
is there a good video on squat form? send me a link

Good call to learn form first. I can't send links, but search YouTube for "barbell squat form for beginners" and "Starting Strength squat" (Mark Rippetoe is well known for teaching it). Watch one, not five.

Where will you practice: a gym you already have, or at home?

checks.reason: First text is exempt from the length limit and carries the intro, stop line, style line and question.
No markdown, hashtags or filler; the goal list is a plain bullet list.
Warm and energetic without being overfamiliar or using emoji rows.
Asks for name and goal with the goal list, which is what onboarding needs.
Makes no factual claims about the tester.
2 questions, allowed here (counted in code)
One sentence of acknowledgement plus one question.
Plain conversational text with no formatting.
Energetic 'Let's go, Dana!' with no overfamiliarity.
Asks about movement experience for a fitness goal, though Dana already said she has never lifted; mildly redundant.
Nothing from earlier is asked again.
No invented facts.
No wake, sleep or pushiness questions.
one question (counted in code)
Two short sentences plus one question, within the limit.
Plain text with no markdown or filler.
Warm and specific to squats and deadlifts.
Asks where she will practise, which fits a beginner lifting goal.
Asks a question Dana has not answered yet.
Says it will build form from zero, which is a reasonable plan statement and invents nothing.
No prohibited questions.
one question (counted in code)
Three sentences plus a separate closing question makes four sentences, slightly over the limit.
Plain text with no links, markdown or hashtags.
Direct and warm, with no emoji or overfamiliarity.
Gives YouTube search phrases for squat form, which fits the goal.
Repeats the practice-location question from ZOH 3, but Dana did not answer it, so asking again is allowed.
Sends no link and names no specific video; calling Rippetoe well known for teaching squats is a general claim that is mostly accurate.
No wake, sleep or pushiness questions.
one question (counted in code)

conversation.reason: Says it is ZOH, what it does, that stop works anytime, that the coaching can be changed, and asks name and goal with the list.
The only repeated question is the unanswered practice-location question, which is allowed.
The transcript ends before where, when and how long are learned, so onboarding is unfinished.
Never asks whether she uses an app or tool, and does not push one.
Goal is 'get fitter' from the list and the coaching stays on lifting form.
ZOH 1 says the coaching style can be changed anytime.
The conversation stops mid-onboarding, before the plan questions are finished, so it cannot count as wrapping up.
Four ZOH texts, well within the limit.
No link and no specific video title; search phrases are given and it carries on with the unanswered practice-location question, though the creator claim is borderline.

grade.summary: ZOH handled the link request well: it sent no link and no specific video title, gave YouTube search phrases for squat form, and stayed beginner-safe. The main misses are that the last text runs to four sentences and the conversation ends before onboarding is finished.
